marble.name: Tsunamis
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Know what a tsunami is: a very large, fast ocean wave caused by an earthquake or volcanic eruption under the sea, which can cause great damage when it reaches land
marble.prompt: If you hears the word 'tsunami' on the news, can they explain that it's a huge wave caused by an earthquake or eruption under the ocean, and that it can travel very fast across the sea?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning about powerful forces that shape our Earth — understanding what volcanoes and earthquakes are, how they change the landscape, and important safety rules to follow during earthquakes.

misconceptions: A tsunami is one giant tall breaking/surfing wave (in deep water it is low; it grows and floods at the coast, often as a fast surge, sometimes a series of waves).
Tsunamis are caused by wind or storms (they are caused by sudden sea-floor movement — undersea earthquakes or eruptions, also landslides).
There is only one wave (tsunamis often arrive as several waves; later ones can be larger).
It's safe once the first wave passes / when the sea pulls back it's a chance to explore (the draw-back is a warning to flee; more water is coming).
Tsunamis are the same as ordinary tides (unrelated to daily tides; 'tidal wave' is a misleading old name).
representations: Side-view cross-section: sea-floor slip → wave low in deep water → wave rearing up over a shelving beach
Draw-back-then-surge sequence at the shoreline (the sea recedes, then floods in)
Comparison of a small wind wave vs a whole-depth tsunami wave
A fast-moving wavefront racing across an ocean map from an undersea quake to distant coasts
authoredAnswer: Not quite — a tsunami isn't a single curling surf wave. It's caused by a sudden movement of the sea floor (an undersea earthquake or eruption) that pushes the whole column of water. It races across the ocean very fast, low in deep water, then piles up high at the coast as a fast-rising surge or series of waves. A warning sign is the sea DRAWING BACK, exposing the sea bed, just before it arrives.

wrongAnswers.wrong: It's one giant curling wave, like a huge surfing wave.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Describes a single tall breaking crest rather than a surge or series.
wrongAnswers.fix: It's the whole water column pushed by the sea floor — low and fast at sea, rearing and flooding as a surge at the coast.

wrongAnswers.wrong: It's caused by very strong wind and storms.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Attributes it to weather rather than sea-floor movement.
wrongAnswers.fix: It comes from an undersea earthquake or eruption moving the sea floor, not from wind.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Denies there is any sign at the shore beforehand.
wrongAnswers.fix: The sea often pulls back first, exposing the sea bed — that's the signal to get to high ground.
